newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea launches cyberspace counterstrike.
newsitem.headline: South Korea launches cyberspace counterstrike.

text.p: South Korea on Wednesday launched a pre-emptive strike against rival North Korea's cyberspace plans, warning users of Pyongyang's planned Internet site that they risked jail terms if the material was distributed.
A North Korean official in Tokyo said the date of the debut of the page on the World Wide Web had not yet been decided, but was likely to be next year.
The official, working at the Korean News Service, the agent in Tokyo of Pyongyang's official Korea Central News Agency (KCNA), said details of the page have not yet been decided.
"KCNA and Korean News Service are negotiating to open a Web site, but timing and other details have not been decided," he said, asking not to be named.
The official denied South Korean reports that KCNA planned to open the Web site on Thursday to mark its 50th anniversary.
"We have not yet decided wether the Web site would be under KCNA or under our news service," he said. The Korean News Service represents pro-Pyongyang Korean residents in Japan.
There has been no announcement by KCNA but Seoul prosecutors wasted no time in ensuring KCNA dispatches, the voice of North Korea's Stalinist leadership, do not circulate in South Korea.

"We still don't know what information KCNA will carry," one prosecution official said. "But if any anti-South Korean propaganda is sent out by a local Internet user, it will violate laws banning such activities and therefore be punished."
South Korea bans distribution of information benefitting North Korea and violators can be jailed for up to seven years.
KCNA stories are a fairly reliable barometer of inter-Korean relations, and lately they have been filled with biting invective against President Kim Young-sam.

On Monday, for example, KCNA carried an item from an official North Korean newspaper describing Kim and the South Korean leadership as "heinous gangsters" and "fascist tyrants" for their crackdown on a pro-Pyongyang student group.
"They are not qualified to live in this world," KCNA said.
The prosecution official denied domestic media reports that authorities have asked Internet providers to block access to North Korea's Internet site.
"Blocking access to Internet sites is difficult and could have serious side effects," he said.

South Korea earlier this year blocked access to a Canadian-based Internet service provider after a Canadian student opened a page carrying North Korean propaganda. It lifted the restriction after the page was closed.
